subjects.name: Rosalind Achterberg
subjects.src: tool:ask_worker:SUPT-SCHOOLS — asked: The school quality index slipped this cycle, with the biggest drops (0.08 to 0.10) in Fruitvale, Grand Lake, Jack London, Uptown, Downtown and West Oakland, while funding and teacher quality held flat

sources.name: Karem Asante
sources.quote: Man, I sit in those meetings and I hear a lot of talk about numbers, but what I see in my one-on-ones is kids carrying stuff they shouldn't have to. The index slipping? That's just a mirror of what they're bringing in—stress from home, from the block, from not knowing if they'll eat tonight. It's not a stat to me; it's their backpacks getting heavier.

sources.name: Rosalind Achterberg
sources.quote: Angela, before I explain anything, I have to correct a premise — and I'd rather do it now than have it in print. **The record I have in front of me doesn't match the numbers in your question.** You cite drops of 0.08 to 0.10 in Fruitvale, Grand Lake, Jack London, Uptown, Downtown and West Oakland. My current sheet shows: - **Fruitvale 7.2**, **Downtown 7.2**, **Jack London 7.3**, **Grand Lake 7.09**, **Uptown 7.03**, **West Oakland 7.92** — with teacher quality flat and funding flat exactly as you describe. But I can't see the prior cycle's rows. My Schools-by-neighborhood record holds this cycle only; it doesn't carry a before-and-after, so I can't independently confirm a 0.08–0.10 slide, and neither can I show you the places where the number held or rose. If your reporter's methodology is comparing against a prior published sheet, I'm not going to dispute your arithmetic — but I'm not going to narrate a dip I can't see the baseline for, either. That's how a superintendent ends up on the record blaming staff for a rounding artifact. Here's what I can say on the record, plainly: **On the numbers.** Teacher quality and funding are held flat across every one of those six neighborhoods — the dollars and the staffing did not move. So whatever moved the index moved *inside* the classroom, not in the budget. And these six are not one story: Fruitvale at 88.2 graduation and West Oakland at 90.5 are performing well above the city's lower tier, while Uptown has 63 students and Grand Lake 319. A tenth of a point on an index with 63 students in the denominator is a handful of students, not a school coming apart. I want your readers to understand the scale of what's being described before they panic about it. **On what my staff are seeing.** I'm not going to invent classroom observations I don't have. What I *do* have from Cycle 117 is residents' own school lines, and they are, candidly, the opposite of a crisis: a Dimond student who asked a question nobody in the room could answer and liked that; a Chinatown student reading ahead in a chapter book; a San Antonio student building a volcano that erupted twice; Jack London and Rockridge students cramming for finals at the library until closing. One Fruitvale student, Karim Avery, was recognized at the Fruitvale Transit Corridor Mutual Aid. That's engaged learning, in the neighborhoods you're asking about. It is also, of course, self-reported and partial — it's not a quality index and I won't dress it up as one. **What I'm actually worried about.** The honest answer is the persistent gap, not the drift. San Antonio at 6.6 and East Oakland at 6.57, both at $11,000 per student, both with the lowest teacher quality in the district at 6.68 — that's a structural problem that a tenth of a point of noise shouldn't distract us from. And I'll flag one thing I own: the Oakland Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline, my $12.5M workforce initiative, has been **stalled since Cycle 116** pending a placement-gap analysis with explicit West Oakland and Fruitvale review, due at Cycle 118. Those are two of the six neighborhoods in your question. When a college-and-career pathway is held up in a neighborhood, that eventually shows up somewhere. I'd rather answer for that than for a tenth of a point. So: put me down as saying the district will publish the prior-cycle comparison alongside this cycle's sheet so the public can see the movement itself rather than my characterization of it, and that I don't yet have a classroom-level explanation that meets the standard of the record. If your sources have something specific in those buildings, I want to hear it — my office line is open.

assert: manifest.approvedFacts are canon — never contradict them
attribute: a named ledger citizen speaks only in manifest.approvedQuotes or their own page line; everyone else speaks in your words
limits.rule: The Packet is what you know, not the fence around what you may write. The approved facts and the ledger are canon: never contradict them, and never import real-world Oakland (its people, businesses, landmarks, troubles). Everything else — the scene, the street, the weather in the room, unnamed people and what they say, new in-world places and businesses, what the city is talking about — is yours to invent; that colour is the job, and it never rewrites a canon fact. A named ledger citizen speaks only in their approved quote or their own page line.
